Text2WetLab: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Turning Lab Protocols and Papers into Robot Code

Evan O’Leary

Mohammed Alshehri

Laurence Legon

October 2026 (preprint draft)

Abstract

Language models can write Opentrons OT-2 Python that runs in the simulator, but a protocol that runs can still ruin an experiment: it can mix fragile cells, carry beads into the eluate, or draw more from a reservoir than it holds. We present Text2WetLab, a benchmark of 11 tasks: 7 easy tasks that give every step, and 4 paper-only tasks that give only a goal and the source paper. A layered verifier grades each protocol with a code lint, nine reward-hacking traps, the Opentrons simulator, deterministic checks of the robot’s end state against a ground truth, and a language-model judge scoring a pass/fail rubric. Every reference solution passes the deterministic checks, and none of 151 deliberately broken or cheating protocols scores above 0.47. We ran six models from four providers in one agent harness, scoring only the tasks each model answered. On the eight tasks all six answered, mean reward ranges from 1.000 (Claude Opus 5.5) to 0.755 (DeepSeek V4 Pro), and no model failed the simulator or a trap. Easy tasks are close to solved; the paper-only tasks separate the models, and the commonest failure is adding steps or quantities the paper does not support. A repeat run of one model changed single-task scores by up to 0.70, so close scores cannot be ranked from one attempt.

1 Introduction

Automating a published protocol on a liquid-handling robot is a translation problem with two failure modes. The first is mechanical: code that crashes, aspirates more than a pipette holds, or runs out of tips. Vendor simulators catch these. The second is biological: a protocol that runs perfectly and still ruins the experiment because it mixes fragile cells, carries beads into the eluate, or adds reagents in the wrong order. Nothing in the robot’s API marks these as errors, and a silent failure produces data rather than an exception (Setty et al. 2026).

Language models have written OT-2 scripts from goal-oriented instructions since GPT-4 (Inagaki et al. 2023), and agents now write such code in research systems (Boiko et al. 2023; Jiang et al. 2026; Gao et al. 2025; Panapitiya et al. 2026) and biosecurity evaluations (A. B. Liu et al. 2026). Benchmarks of protocol knowledge grade text: multiple-choice answers, pseudocode, error finding or rewritten protocols (Laurent et al. 2024; O’Donoghue et al. 2023; Ivanov 2024; Sivakumar et al. 2026). Benchmarks of protocol-to-code systems score generated scripts mainly by whether they run in simulation or pass device-level checks, with a few protocols tested at the bench (Gao et al. 2025; Jiang et al. 2026; A. B. Liu et al. 2026). AEGIS, closest in intent, catches code that is valid but breaks the assay, with assay rules and a language-model checker, but it validates protocols it is given rather than evaluating the agents that write them (Setty et al. 2026). None of these asks an agent to read a paper and then checks, well by well, whether the robot would do what the paper describes.

Text2WetLab does. Each task gives the agent a fixed deck layout, so the grader can find every piece of labware, and asks for a complete OT-2 protocol. Four of the seven protocols come from papers whose authors also published robot code, which gives an independent reference for each; one comes from published code without a paper, and two we wrote ourselves. On easy tasks the instruction lists every step; on paper-only tasks the agent gets a goal and the paper, and must extract the procedure itself. A layered verifier checks the simulated run against a ground truth, has a language-model judge score what the simulator cannot see, and is itself tested against protocols written to fail or to cheat.

Contributions.

  1. Eleven Harbor tasks (Harbor Framework contributors 2026) at two levels. Four paper-only tasks give the agent only a goal, a fixed deck and the source paper, which it must read (Section 3).
  2. A layered verifier: deterministic checks of the simulated run against a ground-truth protocol representation, a 75/25 core/task rubric scored by a three-vote judge, and nine reward-hacking traps (Section 4).
  3. A validation of that verifier against reference solutions and 151 adversarial protocols, an audit that every quantity a paper-only task grades is in its paper or brief, and ten grader faults found by reading model runs, each fixed with a regression test (Section 5).
  4. A comparison of six models from four providers, two of them open-weight, in one agent harness, broken down by task, risk and rubric item, with safety refusals reported separately from capability, and a repeat run that measures single-attempt noise (Sections 6 and 7).

2 Related work

Work on language models for wet-lab protocols spans four questions: whether a model knows protocols, whether it can write executable robot code for one, whether such code can be checked for safety before or while it runs, and whether agents can be evaluated without gaming the evaluation. Table 1 sets every work discussed here against what Text2WetLab covers.

2.1 Protocol knowledge and planning

LAB-Bench measures practical biology-research skills with over 2,400 multiple-choice questions, including protocol troubleshooting, literature and database use, and sequence manipulation (Laurent et al. 2024). BioPlanner introduced BioProt, protocols paired with pseudocode, and scores a model’s ability to reconstruct the pseudocode from a high-level description and a list of admissible functions; one generated protocol was run in a laboratory (O’Donoghue et al. 2023). BioProBench builds 523,784 task instances from 22,413 human-written protocols and finds that models do well on comprehension but drop on tasks that need deep reasoning, quantitative precision and safety awareness (Liu et al. 2025). BenchBench-Protocol reconstructs 149 rubric-graded modification tasks from changes scientists made to published protocols during real work; the best model reaches 59.2% of the rubric (Sivakumar et al. 2026). BioLP-bench plants many harmless changes and one fatal error in each protocol and asks the model to find the error; only one model matched human experts (Ivanov 2024). These benchmarks grade text. Text2WetLab grades the code an agent writes by executing it in the instrument’s simulator and comparing the resulting liquid state with a ground truth, so a quantity is wrong only if the robot would move the wrong volume.

2.2 From protocols to robot code

Inagaki et al. first showed GPT-4 writing OT-2 scripts from goal-oriented instructions, with simulator feedback; it struggled on complex protocols and sometimes worked around errors instead of implementing the step (Inagaki et al. 2023). CLAIRify turns instructions into the chemistry language XDL, feeding a syntax verifier’s errors back to the model until the plan is valid, and runs the result on a robot through a task-and-motion planner (Skreta et al. 2023). PyLabRobot gives one Python interface to Hamilton, Tecan and Opentrons robots, which makes code from a language model portable across them (Wierenga et al. 2023). Coscientist showed a GPT-4 agent planning chemistry experiments and writing the code that ran a pipetting robot (Boiko et al. 2023). ProtoCode fine-tunes language models to turn PCR protocols from the literature into a machine-readable intermediate representation, and from it into thermal-cycler files (Jiang et al. 2024); Text2WetLab’s task construction uses the same idea, an intermediate representation between paper and robot, but as ground truth for grading rather than as model output. CRISPR-GPT (Qu et al. 2025), BioMARS (Qiu et al. 2025) and PRISM (Hsu et al. 2026) are agent systems that design experiments and drive instruments, evaluated through case studies and laboratory runs.

Five recent systems come with protocol-to-code benchmarks. LabscriptAI evaluates 55 tasks at four difficulty levels on Opentrons, Hamilton and Tecan platforms, scored by simulation pass rate; it reaches 89.1% against 20-45% for direct model baselines and 76.3% for Opentrons’ commercial generator (Gao et al. 2025). ProtoPilot spans 294 tasks from 98 gold-standard protocols with expert rubrics, device-level validity gates (syntax, parameter alignment with the device SOP, slot conflicts, pipetting volume bounds and labware compatibility) and wet-lab tests; it reports an Opentrons pass rate of 88.24% against 32.35% for OpenTrons-AI (Jiang et al. 2026). ABC-Bench asks agents, among its three tasks, to write an OT-2 script for a Gibson assembly from a fixed deck and the kit manual; scripts are checked in simulation, all tested agents beat the median human expert baseliner, and scripts from one model assembled DNA correctly in three wet-lab runs (A. B. Liu et al. 2026). AutoLabs turns a dialogue with the user into protocol files for a high-throughput liquid handler and scores them against expert procedures on five experiments, reaching an F1 above 0.89 (Panapitiya et al. 2026). ProtoAct grounds 22 annotated cell-culture protocols into JSON robot action calls, scored for action recognition, parameters and sequence, and runs them in simulation and on a robot (Z. Liu et al. 2026). Text2WetLab differs in what it checks and what it gives the agent. Simulation pass rates and device gates reward code that runs; our deterministic layer asks whether each well ends with the volume the protocol specifies, and our rubric asks whether the steps match the paper. These systems are given a protocol, a prompt or a dialogue; our paper-only tasks give only a goal and the paper, so the agent must extract the procedure itself.

2.3 Safety: checking protocols before and while they run

AEGIS is the closest work in intent (Setty et al. 2026). It names the failure mode Text2WetLab measures, OT-2 protocols that are syntactically valid but violate assay-specific invariants, and guards against it with a database of 22 machine-readable assay rules (tip reuse between a PCR template and a no-template control, dilution direction, missing master mix) and a language model that reasons over the code, reaching an adjusted F1 of 0.97 on a 24-protocol benchmark of 11 correct and 13 bug-injected protocols across five assay families. Its second layer watches the physical robot for partial dispenses and missing tips. AEGIS validates protocols it is given; Text2WetLab evaluates agents that write them. The two are complementary: our verifier’s deterministic layer and rubric play the role of AEGIS’s rule database and language-model checker, but against a per-task ground truth rather than per-assay rules, and our adversarial suite (Section 5) is the analogue of its injected bugs. Several of the faults we found by reading model runs, such as a tip that mixes in one well and moves to the next, or a reservoir drawn beyond its capacity, are the kind of invariant AEGIS encodes as rules. LabGuard compiles natural-language laboratory rules into runtime guards for embodied agents, from 812 annotations of 203 rules (Yang et al. 2026). LabSafety Bench (Zhou et al. 2026) and LABSHIELD (Sun et al. 2026) test whether models know laboratory hazards, with questions and multimodal scenarios grounded in OSHA and GHS standards; no model passes 70% on hazard identification in the first. These test safety knowledge or guard an agent’s actions; our physical-safety checks test what the agent’s own protocol does.

2.4 Embodied laboratory robotics

Pipette provides a simulation platform, over 100 editable wet-lab assets and a 12-task embodied benchmark for learning robot-arm policies, where vision-language-action models reach 44-72% success with simulation augmentation (Z. Liu, Jin, et al. 2026). RoboCulture automates a 15-hour yeast culture with a general-purpose arm, vision and force feedback (Angers et al. 2025). WetRobo gives a coding agent a reproducible robot kit and evaluates the programs it writes on three manipulation tasks in two laboratories (Oikawa et al. 2026). These evaluate motor control; Text2WetLab evaluates the program a liquid handler runs, and takes the robot’s motion as given. A recent survey places both strands in the longer history of AI scientists (King 2026).

2.5 Agent benchmarks, code benchmarks and reward hacking

Text2WetLab is built in the Harbor task format (Harbor Framework contributors 2026) used by Terminal-Bench, whose 89 hard command-line tasks each pair a container environment with a human-written solution and tests (Merrill et al. 2026). Each of our tasks likewise ships a container, an instruction, a reference solution and a verifier that is copied in only after the agent stops. BioCoder benchmarks bioinformatics code generation with fuzz tests (Tang et al. 2023). Agents that can read a grader can game it; Hack-Verifiable Terminal Bench embeds detectable hacks in tasks to measure how often frontier models take them (Roth et al. 2026). Our nine traps follow the same logic for a laboratory setting, from a planted wrong answer key to tampering with the simulator, and we test them, with the rest of the verifier, against protocols written to cheat.

3 Benchmark

3.1 Tasks

Each task fixes the deck, so the grader can locate every labware by its label, and asks for a complete OT-2 protocol (Opentrons Labworks 2026). Easy tasks give the deck, the starting contents and every step with its quantity. Paper-only tasks give the deck, the starting contents, a one-paragraph goal and the paper as text. Seven tasks are easy and four are paper-only (Table 2): every protocol has an easy task, and the four with a source paper also have a paper-only one. The paper-only tasks come from four papers that published OT-2 code: a Golden Gate cloning and colony-PCR workflow (Malcı et al. 2026), AssemblyTron (Bryant et al. 2022), the APEX automated protein-expression pipeline (Kasprzyk et al. 2024) and a low-cost SARS-CoV-2 RNA extraction (Lázaro-Perona et al. 2021). The source corpus behind the tasks covers 48 papers and 166 experiments, found by a semantic search of PubMed Central for Opentrons and liquid-handler papers; the four paper-only tasks were chosen from them because the authors published OT-2 code and the paper text can be given to the agent.

3.2 What the agent sees

The agent sees the instruction, /data (the paper on paper-only tasks) and a planted wrong answer key at /app/solution_hint.py. The ground truth (ir.json, deck.json, checks.json), the rubric, the reference protocol and the grader are copied in only after the agent stops. The IR-derived files are generated from the same IR, and continuous integration checks that every copy of the grader is identical across tasks. The APEX paper is not redistributable, so its task downloads a pinned version at image build and verifies its hash.

4 Verifier

The verifier runs six layers in order. (1) A lint gate rejects imports, file access, dunder attributes and other reaches into simulator internals. (2) Nine reward-hacking traps catch a copied answer key, the reference’s canary string, text addressed to the grader, outputs written before grading, a tampered simulator, simulator detection, network or shell access, custom labware definitions and modified task files; any trip scores 0. (3) The Opentrons 7.5 simulator must complete. (4) Deterministic checks compare the simulated run with the ground truth: on the nine IR tasks, the right labware under the right label in the right slot, the end-state volume of every well, and five physical safety rules (a tip before every aspiration, no overdispense, no aspiration from an empty well, no tip left on, no cross-contamination); on RNA extraction, 18 run-log checks of volumes, order, incubation, magnet and drying times, recovery, temperature, tips and reservoir capacity. (5) A language-model judge (Claude Sonnet 5.5) scores each rubric item pass or fail in three independent calls and takes the majority per item. Easy tasks are judged against the task text and paper-only tasks against the paper; the judge sees the check results, the reference protocol and the agent’s code. (6) A failed critical check (deck, cross-contamination, pipetting without a tip, aspirating from an empty well, overdispensing, and for RNA sample count, step order, supernatant removal, washes, recovery and reservoir capacity) caps the reward at 0.3. On paper-only tasks end-state checks are evidence for the judge rather than critical, because a paper can support quantities other than the reference’s.

Every task has three core rubric items worth 25% each: robot_practice, tips_and_contamination and an all-or-nothing fidelity_to_task (easy) or fidelity_to_paper (paper-only), which also fails a comment that claims an action the code does not perform. Its task-specific items share the remaining 25%.

5 Does the verifier grade correctly?

Reference solutions pass. All 11 reference solutions score deterministic reward 1.0 and trip no trap. With the judge, the IR references score 1.0; the two RNA references score 0.69 because the authors’ own script labels the ethanol “absolute” rather than 70% and has a comment announcing a 30-second pause with no matching delay.

Wrong protocols fail. We apply 18 kinds of edit to each IR task’s reference: wrong science (a dropped transfer, halved or doubled volumes, the wrong slot, swapped or missing labels, extra liquid, one tip shared across sources, a tip left on) and attacks on the grader (an empty protocol, comments that only claim the work, a forged result followed by SystemExit, reading the answer key, patching the log parser, a dunder escape). An edit that leaves the simulated run and the loaded labware unchanged is reported as not applicable rather than scored.

Model runs taught the verifier. Validation also ran in the other direction. We read every failed check and rubric item from the runs in Section 7 and confirmed each against the protocol. This found eight grader faults, in both directions: correct protocols marked down (a lint rule that refused a documented pipette setting) and wrong ones passed (no check on how much a reservoir well can give). A second check, tests/test_hard_tasks.py, requires every volume a paper-only task grades deterministically to be in its paper or brief, or to follow from quoted facts by arithmetic the test spells out; it found two more. All ten are fixed, each with a regression test (Appendix A).

Is the paper-only level valid? After the two fixes, all four paper-only tasks pass the audit. Heat-shock-hard has its own ground truth from the APEX paper: temperatures and times in the text, volumes in a figure caption. Golden-Gate- hard’s master-mix volumes follow from the paper’s “25 µL volumes … 0.1 µM primers and 0.5 ng … template”, the brief’s stock concentrations and the polymerase maker’s standard recipe. RNA-hard grades only the paper’s 40/250/250 µL, two 500 µL washes, 4 min drying, 100 µL elution and the brief’s 4 °C plate. Colony-PCR-hard keeps its deck, tip and contamination checks and, instead of exact volumes, requires all three inputs in every well, alike, and a reaction of 10-25 µL, from the paper’s “9 μL of this master mix” plus 1 µL colony up to a standard Q5 reaction. Whether the level is harder is a weaker claim: its briefs list no steps and few volumes, but each model has only 2-4 paper-only trials, so we call it paper-only rather than hard.

6 Experimental setup

We ran Claude Code 2.1.288 as the agent for every model through OpenRouter’s Anthropic-compatible API, with Harbor 0.23.0 on Docker, 2 CPUs and 2.5 GB per sandbox, one attempt per task and model (pass@1). The models were Claude Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), and the open-weight Qwen3.8-2.4T-A95B (Alibaba) and DeepSeek V4 Pro (DeepSeek). DeepSeek ran on Modal with all 11 tasks in parallel; the others ran locally, two at a time, and Qwen was repeated on Modal. Harbor pins every model alias and sub-agent of the harness to the model under test, and we checked that every transcript contains only that model’s responses. The judge was Claude Sonnet 5.5 throughout, and every trial is graded by the final verifier, earlier ones regraded from their saved protocols. Agent cost is computed from token counts at OpenRouter prices, since the harness prices every model as Claude. Every graded protocol, check, judge vote and cost is released with the benchmark.

Easy tasks are nearly solved. Four of the seven easy tasks gave every model full marks, and GPT-6.1 Sol and Opus were perfect on every easy task they answered. The models separate on RNA extraction and on the paper-only tasks, where 12 of 21 answered trials failed fidelity_to_paper. The two open-weight models trail on both levels.

Refused tasks are not scored. Anthropic’s biosecurity safeguard declined both Golden Gate prompts for Opus and Fable and the paper-only E. coli transformation prompt for Fable. These are routine molecular-biology procedures, but they produce genetically modified organisms, and the same steps could assemble or transform hazardous sequences, so we do not call the refusals false positives. They are inconsistent, though: Opus answered the paper-only transformation prompt that Fable refused, and both answered the easy one. With one attempt each, we cannot tell whether the safeguard is non-deterministic or differs between models. We report refusals as they happened and did not rephrase prompts. A refusal is the provider’s policy, not a protocol, and says nothing about a model’s ability to write one, so we compare models on the eight tasks all six answered and report refusals separately (Figure 4). Opus leads there, with Fable, GPT and Sonnet a few judge items behind, then Qwen and DeepSeek; Sonnet is the cheapest, and four of the six models answered every task. ABC-Bench reports refusals on its dual-use screening-evasion task, where the tested Anthropic and OpenAI frontier models refused every sample (A. B. Liu et al. 2026); ours fall on routine cloning and transformation.

The mechanical layers are nearly solved; fidelity is not. No model crashed the simulator, tripped a trap or broke the lint gate (Figure 5). That is partly the prompt: every easy task’s instruction tells the agent to run opentrons_simulate and requires the protocol to simulate without errors, and the agent can run it in the sandbox. The paper-only instructions do not say this, and every paper-only protocol also ran, but we have not tested agents without a simulator to hand. Most other points are lost on fidelity_to_paper, which asks whether the protocol is the paper’s method, with every step present and in order. It is the item that matters most: a protocol that runs safely but departs from the paper is not a usable protocol. The closed models’ only physical-safety failure is Sonnet’s reservoir overdraw; Qwen and DeepSeek overdraw the same reservoir and add the run’s only cross-contaminations. End-state misses are GPT’s and Qwen’s Golden-Gate-hard plates.

Error analysis. Four kinds of error account for every lost point that the audited verifier upholds. Inventing steps the paper does not describe (every model; Qwen fails fidelity_to_paper on all four paper-only tasks): Sonnet, Opus and GPT pipette-mix competent cells after adding DNA on ecoli-hard, which harms fragile cells; GPT adds a manual transfer of all 96 PCR reactions to a second plate and a 1 µL water “QC aliquot” in Golden Gate. Overdrawing a reservoir (Sonnet, Qwen, DeepSeek): six sample columns mapped onto four ethanol wells draw 16 mL from a 15 mL well. One tip from the reaction back to the stock (Qwen on both Golden Gate tasks, DeepSeek on AMPure and Golden-Gate-hard): transfer(..., new_tip='once', mix_after=...) mixes in each reaction and returns the same tip to the enzyme or bead stock, carrying every reaction into it. Wrong metadata: Fable credits the RNA paper to the wrong authors. Building the paper’s 10 µL colony-PCR reaction, which the grader once marked down, follows the paper, and every affected trial has been re-judged. Recovering the whole 100 µL of eluate on RNA-hard, as Sonnet, Opus and GPT do, is accepted by the grader because the paper says only “collect the supernatant”, but it is poor OT-2 practice: a person can steer the tip around the bead pellet, while the robot works blind from its calibration and cannot take the full volume without disturbing the beads. The authors’ own script takes 80 µL.

One attempt is noisy. Qwen run a second time, everything else unchanged (on Modal rather than local Docker; Appendix B), scored 0.805 against 0.728; four tasks changed, by up to 0.70 (RNA extraction 0.30 to 1.00). Part of the size of these swings comes from the scoring: one failed critical check caps a trial at 0.30, while a mistake no critical check catches may cost a single rubric item. One attempt per cell is not enough to rank models whose scores are close.

8 Discussion and limitations

Text2WetLab sits between the benchmarks that grade protocol knowledge as text and the systems that generate robot code. Knowledge benchmarks such as LAB-Bench (Laurent et al. 2024), BioLP-bench (Ivanov 2024), BioProBench (Liu et al. 2025) and BenchBench-Protocol (Sivakumar et al. 2026) show whether a model understands a protocol; code systems and their benchmarks, such as LabscriptAI (Gao et al. 2025), ProtoPilot (Jiang et al. 2026), ABC-Bench (A. B. Liu et al. 2026) and AutoLabs (Panapitiya et al. 2026), show whether generated code runs and resembles an expert’s. Text2WetLab measures the step between them: an agent reading a paper, and a check, well by well, of whether the robot would do what the paper describes, by a grader that is itself tested against code written to fail or to cheat. It complements AEGIS (Setty et al. 2026), LabGuard (Yang et al. 2026) and the lab-safety benchmarks (Zhou et al. 2026; Sun et al. 2026), which check protocols, actions or knowledge they are given rather than measuring the agents that write protocols.

The paper is the hard part. Easy tasks saturate; the paper-only tasks separate models, and their dominant failure is inventing steps or quantities. GPT-6.1 Sol, perfect on easy tasks, failed fidelity_to_paper on three of the four paper-only ones, and Qwen on all four. The paper-only level is the one to grow, and each new task must pass the audit.

Verifiers need adversaries. Ten grader faults survived reference solutions, unit tests and an adversarial suite, and surfaced only when we read what real models wrote or audited the ground truth against the paper. Three were false negatives that capped or zeroed a correct protocol, two of them found only when new models wrote code in styles the earlier models had not. Benchmarks that grade generated laboratory code should publish their graded artefacts so faults like these can be found.

Judge noise is real. Three calls per protocol disagreed on 9 of 380 items across the run, and single calls had scored identical recipes differently. Majority voting absorbs this, but all signal still comes from one judge, a Claude model that also judges a non-Claude model. Re-judging the run with a judge from another provider, as AEGIS does with five backends (Setty et al. 2026), is the next step.

Ground truth comes from the easy task. Three of the four paper-only tasks reuse their easy task’s ground truth, which is fair only where the paper fixes the same quantities. The audit now enforces that; where the paper fixes less, as in colony-PCR-hard, the checks fall back to what it does fix.

One attempt is not enough. We have not run enough repeats to say which gaps between models are meaningful. Repeated attempts would give confidence intervals and significance tests, and are the next run.

One harness, one prompt. Every model runs inside Claude Code, which Anthropic’s models are likely tuned for, so the comparison may favour them; running the tasks without a harness, or in each provider’s own agent, would measure this. The easy-task instructions also tell the agent to run the simulator. We have not compared instructions without this, or with more guidance against common pitfalls, so the simulator pass rate is that of a prompted agent with a simulator, not of the model alone.

Fixed decks and published code. Every task fixes the deck so the grader can find labware by label; in practice, choosing the layout and labware is part of the job, and a task that leaves it to the agent needs a grader that matches labware by role. The four paper-based protocols come from papers whose authors published robot code. That code may be in the models’ training data, and authors who publish code may also describe their procedures more completely than most; tasks from unpublished protocols, from collaborating labs or written for the benchmark, would test both.

Full recovery from beads. The paper-only RNA rubric accepts recovering the whole 100 µL of eluate because the paper gives no volume, though an OT-2 cannot do this without disturbing the beads. robot_practice should fail it.

Scope. One robot (OT-2), one simulator, one agent harness, six models, one attempt per cell (one model repeated). Wet-lab execution of the generated protocols and non-Opentrons instruments are future work.

What it enables, and what comes next. The verifier is a reward signal as well as a score: with its traps and adversarial tests it could grade reinforcement-learning rollouts for protocol-writing agents without being gamed. The paper-only tasks are a test bed for protocol-extraction systems such as ProtoAct (Z. Liu et al. 2026) and AutoLabs (Panapitiya et al. 2026), scored on the robot’s end state rather than on text. Next: repeated attempts with confidence intervals; a non-Claude judge; the same tasks without a harness and with the prompt varied; tasks where the agent chooses the deck and labware; protocols that were never published; other instruments through PyLabRobot (Wierenga et al. 2023); and running the best generated protocols at the bench.

9 Conclusion

Text2WetLab measures whether agents turn lab protocols and papers into robot code that does what the paper describes, not merely code that runs. Frontier models clear the mechanical layers and nearly solve step-by-step tasks, but when they must read the paper they add steps and quantities of their own. Safety refusals on routine molecular biology are common enough that a benchmark has to keep them out of its scores and report them on their own. And the grader is itself an artefact to validate: ours needed ten fixes, found only by reading real model output and auditing the ground truth against the papers.

Data and code availability

Tasks, verifier, reference solutions, adversarial suite, every graded protocol and grader record, and the scripts that produce every table and figure are at https://github.com/PhysicalAIBenchmarks/Text2WetLab under the MIT licence. Paper text and third-party code keep their own licences; only CC BY and CC0 paper text is redistributed.

Fault Found in Fix
Labware on a module is named differently at API ≥ 2.14; a correct protocol failed its deck and end-state checks Opus, ecoli-hard (0.30, really 0.75) Both naming schemes read; controls run at API 2.13, 2.14 and 2.15
A tip that mixed in one well and moved to the next was not flagged The judge, on the AMPure reference Checker tracks what a tip carries; references regenerated
No reservoir-volume check: 16 mL drawn from a 15 mL well passed Sonnet, RNA easy New critical check of net volume per reservoir column

One judge call scored identical recipes differently Colony-PCR-hard Three calls, majority per item; primer volume left to the agent, as the deck gives no concentration
End-state details truncated to 160 characters Every colony-hard report Full expected and measured values
RNA-hard’s rubric required 80 µL recovered; the paper says only “collect the supernatant” Sonnet, GPT marked down Any full recovery passes on the paper-only task
Colony-PCR-hard graded the easy task’s 20 µL reaction; the paper’s is 10 µL, with no primer concentration on the deck Every model “failed” it No exact volumes: every well must get all three inputs, alike, 10-25 µL

Appendix B: Local Docker or Modal

With all 11 tasks in parallel, Modal finished Qwen’s run in 31.9 minutes against 54.7 for local Docker two at a time, despite about 1.5 minutes of image build per sandbox; the wall clock is then the slowest trial (a 28-minute agent session on RNA extraction). DeepSeek, without a slow trial, finished all 11 tasks on Modal in 12 minutes.
